text: Dear Sam, I'm 13 and I live in Braga. This year my best friend Inês is different. She sits with a new group in the canteen and she hardly answers my messages. Last week they made a group chat for a party and I wasn't in it. I felt really left out. I'm not angry, just confused. Rita

slides.title: "Someone stole my account"
text: Last spring, Duarte, 14, from Coimbra, got a message from a "friend": vote for my band, just enter your login here. He did. Ten minutes later he couldn't open his account. The hacker changed his password and sent the same link to all his contacts.

"I felt stupid," he says. His sister helped him report the account, and he got it back after two days. Now he uses two-step verification and a different password for every app. "If a message feels urgent, I stop and check."

slides.title: Meet Leonor, 14, surfer
text: Leonor lives in Ericeira and goes surfing almost every day before school. "I wake up at 6.30, check the waves on my phone and run to the beach with my board."

In winter the water is freezing, so she wears a thick wetsuit. On weekdays she trains for an hour, and on Saturdays she does yoga to stay flexible. She never drinks fizzy drinks and goes to bed at ten. "My friends think I'm crazy, but when I catch a good wave, I feel free."

slides.title: Uluru: a rock with a soul
text: In the red desert of central Australia there is a giant rock called Uluru. At sunset it changes colour from orange to deep red, and thousands of tourists come to see it.

For the Anangu, the Aboriginal people of the area, Uluru is a sacred place full of ancient stories and paintings. For years, visitors climbed it, but the Anangu asked them not to. Since 2019, climbing Uluru has been forbidden. Today tourists walk around the base instead and learn about Anangu culture.

chapters.title: The Account with No Face
paragraphs: My name is Tomás Ferreira. I'm thirteen, I live in Matosinhos, and I have made forty-three videos for my YouTube channel, Tomás Tries Things. The channel has got forty-one subscribers. Twelve of them are relatives. One of them is my grandmother, who has never watched a single video because she thinks YouTube is something you catch in winter.

On the first day of 8.º ano I got up at seven, put on my least terrible T-shirt and walked to school with Inês. Inês Carvalho has been my best friend since nursery, so we have known each other for about ten years. In that time she has beaten me at chess more than three hundred times. I have beaten her once. She had a temperature of thirty-nine.
"Have you finished your summer video yet?" she asked.
"Almost. I've just got to edit the bit where I fall off the paddleboard."
"You've already posted that bit. Twice."
"That was a teaser."

Our school is five minutes from the beach, which means two things. First, the classrooms smell of grilled sardines until October. Second, the seagulls are enormous and they have no manners. Last year one of them stole a whole bifana out of Rafa Lopes's hand. He has never got over it. He says it looked him in the eye first.

Rafa was already in the classroom when we arrived. He was sitting on a desk and showing everyone a video of himself doing keepy-uppies. "Three hundred views in one hour," he said. "I'm basically famous, aren't I?"
"Basically," said Inês, without looking up.

Then Professora Lemos came in. She is our English teacher, she has taught at the school for twenty years and she says "Brilliant!" about everything, even when Rafa writes the date in the wrong place. Behind her there was a girl I didn't know. She was tall, with sun-bleached hair tied up in a messy knot, and she was wearing a blue hoodie with a big fish on the front.
"Everyone, this is Kiara Walsh," said Professora Lemos. "She has just arrived from Perth, in Australia. Be nice. Brilliant."
Rafa put his hand up. He didn't wait for permission. "So you've got a pet kangaroo, haven't you?"
A few people laughed. Kiara didn't. She looked at Rafa the way scientists look at insects. "No. Have you got a pet sardine?"
"What? No."
"Weird. I thought everyone in Portugal had one."
This time the whole class laughed, and they weren't laughing with Rafa. Even Professora Lemos had to look out of the window for a moment. Rafa went red and pretended to check his phone.

Kiara sat at the empty desk next to mine. She spoke Portuguese with a funny accent, half Porto and half something sunnier. At break she told us that her dad was Australian and her mum had grown up in Perth, but her grandmother was born here, in Matosinhos.
"She went to this school, actually," Kiara said. "A long time ago."
"Cool," I said, because I am a brilliant conversationalist.
Rafa spent the rest of break doing a kangaroo impression for anyone who would watch. It looked more like a nervous chicken.
"You're staring at her," Inês whispered later, in Maths.
"I'm not staring. I'm observing. For content."
"You've written her name in your notebook. With a little wave next to it."
I closed my notebook.
After school we found out that Kiara and I were neighbours. There was a moving van outside the building opposite mine, and two men were carrying a surfboard up the stairs very carefully, like a baby.
"You live there?" I asked.
"Since Saturday. Third floor." She pointed. "What about you?"
"There. Second floor. With my mum and my avó."
Kiara looked up at my building for a long time, longer than any building deserves. Then she smiled in a way I didn't understand and said, "See you tomorrow, Tomás."

My avó, Fátima, has lived in our flat all her life. She has seen everything, she says, and she hasn't liked much of it. That evening she was making caldo verde and complaining about the new neighbours. "They've put a surfboard on the balcony," she said. "A surfboard! It's going to fall on someone's head, isn't it?"
"Maybe the seagulls will take it," I said.
Avó looked at me as if I had said something stupid, which is how she looks at me most of the time. "Seagulls take bifanas, Tomás. Not surfboards. Don't be ridiculous."
I was in my room, setting up my camera for a new video, when my phone started to buzz. Then it buzzed again. Then it didn't stop. Our class group chat had exploded.
"Has anyone else been followed by this weird account??" Rafa wrote.

The account was called @gaivota_79. It had no profile picture, only a drawing of a seagull, and it followed everyone in 8.º B. It had one post: an old black-and-white photo of our school gate. The trees were smaller and the cars outside looked like toys, but it was definitely our gate. Under it, in English, there was a caption: "I've been away for a long time. Have you missed me? Clue 1: Look for the boy who has never lost a game."
"Don't click on any links," Inês wrote. "Don't follow it back. It's probably a bot."
"A bot that knows our school?? It's a ghost, isn't it," wrote Rafa.
"Ghosts don't use Instagram, Rafa."
Diogo sent a skull. Beatriz sent seven question marks. Someone asked if it was the school's new Instagram account, and Inês replied that the school's account only posts photos of soup.

I looked at that photo for an hour. I zoomed in on every corner. I couldn't find anything strange, except the fact that someone had taken a picture of our school in 1979 and had decided to show it to a class of thirteen-year-olds forty-seven years later.

At 23:47 my phone buzzed again. A new post. This time it was an old photo of a building I knew very well, because I was inside it. It was my building. On the second floor, a girl with dark plaits was leaning out of a window. My window.
The caption said: "You've lived here all your life, haven't you, Tomás?"

I went to the window. The street was empty. All the windows across the road were dark. On the railing of my balcony, a huge seagull was sitting perfectly still, staring at me as if it had just read all my messages.

chapters.title: Don't Feed the Gull
paragraphs: I didn't sleep much that night. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw that seagull. At three in the morning I got up and closed the curtains. At four I opened them again, because it's worse when you can't see.
In the morning I showed the photo to Mum while she was looking for her car keys. She stopped looking for her keys, which shows you how serious it was.
"Have you replied to it?" she asked.
"No."
"Have you clicked on anything?"
"No. I've only looked at it. A lot."

"Good. Don't answer it, don't follow it and don't delete anything. We're going to report it, and I'm going to call your school." She took a screenshot with her own phone, which felt very professional for someone who still couldn't find her keys.

Professora Lemos had already heard about the account. Half the school had heard about it. By the second lesson, @gaivota_79 had two hundred followers and Rafa had told everyone that the ghost of a dead student had chosen me personally.
"Nobody has died," said Professora Lemos. "Brilliant. Now, phones on the desks, please."
For the next fifty minutes we talked about online safety. It was the most interesting lesson we have ever had, mainly because it was about us.
"Has anyone here ever accepted a follow request from a stranger?" she asked.
About twenty hands went up, slowly. Rafa's went up first. "I've accepted everyone," he said proudly. "More followers."
"And how many of those followers have you actually met?"
Rafa started counting on his fingers. Then he stopped counting.

"The rule is simple," said Professora Lemos. "If something online makes you feel scared or uncomfortable, you don't deal with it alone. You tell an adult you trust. You report it. You block it if you want. You never share your address or your timetable. And you don't feed the gull."
"Feed the gull?"
"Answer it. Give it attention. That's what it wants, isn't it?"

Then she showed us how to make an account private and how to check which apps can see our location. Inês already knew everything, obviously. I discovered that my phone has shared my location with a cooking app since I was eleven. I have never cooked anything in my life.
Kiara didn't say anything during the lesson. At break she sat with Inês and me on the wall near the canteen, eating an apple very slowly.
"Are you scared?" she asked me.
"Me? No. I've seen much worse things."
"Like what?"
"Rafa's dance videos."
She laughed, but she was watching me carefully, like someone who wanted to see what I would do next.

By then, some people in our class had already decided who the gull was. Diogo said it was a hacker, probably from another country. Beatriz said it was a girl, because boys can't write such neat captions. Rafa looked at Kiara and said, "It started the day the new girl arrived. That's a bit strange, isn't it?"
"Oh, sure," said Kiara. "In Australia we learn hacking at school. Between surfing and wrestling crocodiles."
"Really?" said Rafa.
Inês closed her eyes for a long time.
Inês doesn't believe in ghosts, but she believes in puzzles. At lunch she drew the clue on a napkin: Look for the boy who has never lost a game.
"The trophy cabinet," I said. "The futsal team from the eighties?"
"I've already checked. They lost loads of games." She tapped the napkin. "Think, Tomás. Who has never lost a game?"
"Someone who's never played one," said Kiara quietly.

Inês turned to the window. In the school garden, next to the old gym, there is a small stone statue of a boy with a ball under his arm. He has stood there for as long as anyone can remember. Birds sit on his head. People hang their jackets on his arm. Nobody looks at him.
"He's been there for about fifty years," said Inês slowly, "and he has never played a game in his life."

After the last lesson the three of us went to the garden. We looked around the statue, under it and behind it. We moved some leaves and pulled out a crisp packet and a very old chewing gum. I was ready to give up when Kiara knelt down and brushed the moss off the back of the stone.
Someone had scratched letters into it, a long time ago. They were small and uneven, as if they were done with a key: L + F 1979. AMIGAS PARA SEMPRE.
"Friends forever," Kiara translated, very softly. Her face had changed. She looked as if she had just found something she had lost.
"What are you lot doing behind my statue?"
We all jumped. It was Sr. Albano, the caretaker, holding a broom like a sword.
"It isn't your statue," said Inês.
"I've looked after that boy for thirty years. He's more mine than yours. Out!"

We ran all the way to the gate, which is not easy when you're laughing. At the gate my phone buzzed. A new post from @gaivota_79, a close-up of the letters we had just found: "You've found my first secret, haven't you? Well done. But you haven't found the important one yet."
I looked around. The street was full of parents, scooters and pigeons. Kiara had her hands in the pocket of her hoodie and was looking at the sea.
That night at dinner I showed Avó Fátima the photo of the letters. She went to my school too, and I thought she might know who L and F were.
"Avó, look. Someone wrote this in 1979. You were at the school then, weren't you?"

She was carrying a plate of fried fish. She looked at the screen. The plate hit the floor and broke into three pieces. My grandmother has never dropped anything in her life. She once caught a falling glass with her foot.
"Where did you get that?" she asked, in a voice I had never heard before.
I didn't have time to answer. She went into her bedroom and closed the door, and for the first time in my life I heard my grandmother cry.

chapters.title: Take It Down
paragraphs: Avó Fátima didn't come out of her room that night. In the morning she made my toast as usual, with too much butter, and said nothing. When I opened my mouth, she pointed the butter knife at me. "Não," she said. In Avó's language that means: not now, not ever, eat your toast.

For three weeks nothing happened. The gull didn't post. Mum reported the account and the school sent a letter to all the parents about online safety, which Mum read aloud at dinner. Twice. @gaivota_79 now had nine hundred followers, and people had started to forget about it. I hadn't.
Then I made a mistake. A big one.

I made a video called The Gull Mystery: What We've Found So Far. It had dramatic music, slow zooms on the statue and a beautiful shot of Inês reading the clue in the garden with the wind in her hair. I uploaded it on a Friday night without asking her. By Saturday morning it had two thousand views. My channel has never had so many views. My channel has never had so many anything.
On Monday it was the school Magusto, when everybody stands around a fire in the playground, eats roast chestnuts and gets their hands black. I found Inês next to the fire. She didn't say hello.
"You've put my face on the internet," she said. "Without asking me."
"It's a good shot! You look like a detective."
"I look like a target, Tomás. You've shown everyone the statue. You've shown everyone our school. You've shown the gull exactly what we know. Have you even thought about that?"
"It's just a video."

"Two thousand people have watched it. Somebody wrote a comment about my teeth, and somebody else wrote something I'm not going to repeat." Her eyes were shiny, and it wasn't the smoke. "Take it down."
"Inês..."
"Take. It. Down."
She walked away and left her chestnuts on the wall. Inês never leaves chestnuts.

I took the video down that night. It didn't help. For two weeks she sat with Beatriz in English and walked to school ten minutes earlier than me. I have known Inês for ten years and we have never had a real fight, not even when I sat on her chess set and broke the white queen. It turned out that a real fight feels like a stomach ache that slowly moves up into your chest.

Kiara was the one who sat with me during those weeks. December was coming, and she was homesick in a way that made her very quiet. At break she showed me photos of her friends in Perth, all of them in shorts.

"At home Christmas is in summer," she said. "We go to the beach in the morning and then we have a barbecue. Prawns, salads, pavlova. Then Dad falls asleep in the sun and gets burnt. Every year! He has never learned."
"Here we eat bacalhau on Christmas Eve," I said. "With boiled potatoes and cabbage. Then Avó says the bacalhau was better in the old days."
"Was it?"
"Everything was better in the old days. Ask Avó."
She laughed. Then she sighed. "You know what people here ask me? If I've ever touched a koala. If there are spiders in my shoes. If everyone in Australia surfs."
"And does everyone surf?"
"I surf. That's different." She threw her apple core at a pigeon and missed. "Have you said sorry to Inês?"
"I've taken the video down."
"That isn't what I asked, is it?"

I thought about it for two days. I wrote Inês a long message, deleted it, wrote a shorter one and deleted that too. In the end I didn't send anything. On Saturday I knocked on her door with her favourite chocolate and my chess set, the one with the glued queen.
"I was wrong," I said. "I didn't think about you. I only thought about the views. I'm sorry."
She looked at me for a long time. Then she took the chocolate.
"White or black?" she said.
That's how Inês says "I forgive you". She beat me in eleven moves. Then she beat me again in nine, just to make sure I had understood.

On the last day of term there was a Christmas party in the canteen, with fake snow on the windows and a Christmas jumper competition that Rafa lost to a teacher. Inês, Kiara and I were sharing a plate of rabanadas when every phone in the room buzzed at the same time.

@gaivota_79 had posted again. It was an old photo of the inside of our gym. The far wall was covered with a huge painting of a blue wave, but the photo was blurry and half of it was in shadow. The caption said: "Clue 2: Behind the wall that was painted twice, the sea is waiting. Hurry up. Time is running out."
"Running out for what?" said Rafa, with his mouth full.
Nobody knew. Our gym has white walls. It has always had white walls. Inês ate her rabanada in one bite and said nothing, which is what she does when her brain is working.
On Christmas Eve, after the bacalhau, Mum went to the kitchen to make coffee and Avó Fátima suddenly started talking, as if someone had pressed a button.

"L was Lurdes," she said. "She lived across the street. We were best friends from the age of six. We did everything together. Then in the summer of 1980 her family emigrated. She left without saying goodbye. One morning their flat was just empty."
"Have you ever talked to her since then?"
"Never."
"Where did she go?"
"Away," said Avó, which is not a country. Then she got up, cleared the table, and the conversation was over.
On Boxing Day, Inês called me at nine in the morning, which is a crime in the holidays.

"I've found out something," she said. "The gull's photos aren't scans. They're photos of old photos, taken with a phone. And in the gym photo, there's a reflection on the glossy paper. Zoom in on the top corner."
I zoomed in. There was a tiny reflection of a window, with a balcony and green railings.
"Green railings like that," said Inês, "only exist on one street in Matosinhos. Tomás, the gull lives on your street."

chapters.title: The Man with the Drone
paragraphs: If you live on the same street for thirteen years, you think you know everybody on it. You don't. You know the people who say hello. The rest are just doors.

In the first week of January, Inês, Kiara and I sat on my bedroom floor with a pizza box and a marker, and we made a list of everyone who lived on our street. Inês called it the suspect board. I called it a pizza box.

Number 8: Dona Rosário, who feeds every cat in Matosinhos and talks to them in French. Number 10: Sr. Pinto, whose dog barks at buses but never at burglars. Number 12, first floor, right under my flat: an Airbnb, which is always full of tourists who drag their suitcases over the cobbles at six in the morning. Number 11, third floor: Kiara.
"You can't put me on the list," said Kiara. "I'm a detective."
"Everyone is on the list," said Inês, and she wrote: Kiara (detective?). Kiara laughed, a bit too loudly.

Inês explained her theory with the marker. "If you take a photo of a glossy photo, the light makes a reflection. If there's a reflection, there's a window. And if the window has green railings, it's on this street. It's simple."
"Then why haven't we solved it?"
"Because there are forty-two windows on this street. I've counted them."

That week the Airbnb had three guests. The first two were Mr and Mrs Medeiros, a retired couple from Toronto, whose parents had left the Azores for Canada in the 1960s. I met them on the stairs. They were wearing matching raincoats and holding a map, which nobody does any more.
"Excuse me, young man," said Mrs Medeiros in careful Portuguese. "Is it far to the bookshop that looks like Harry Potter?"
"Livraria Lello? It's in Porto. If you take the metro, you'll be there in half an hour. But if you go now, you'll queue for an hour."
"And if we go early tomorrow?"
"Then you'll queue for an hour tomorrow."

Mr Medeiros laughed. They told me that in Toronto there is a whole neighbourhood where you can buy pastéis de nata and hear fado on a Saturday night. Their grandchildren speak English at home, learn French at school, because Canada has two official languages, and know about twenty words of Portuguese, all of them food.
"People think every Canadian plays ice hockey," said Mr Medeiros. "I do, but that's not the point."
The third guest was Josh, a tall American with a beard, a backpack the size of a fridge and a drone.

Meanwhile, Kiara had a new hobby: trying to get me into the sea. On Saturday mornings she trained with the school surf team at Matosinhos beach, and she came back with salty hair and an annoyingly good mood.
"You should come next week."
"It's January. The water is fourteen degrees."
"That's why wetsuits exist."
"If I went into that water, I'd die. Honestly. My heart would stop."
"If you went to bed before two in the morning, you'd have more energy."

That was unfair. It was true, but it was unfair. During the holidays I had played video games until three almost every night, I had eaten mainly crisps and I had walked about as far as the fridge. My lifestyle, as Mum said, was more sofa than style.
On Saturday evening the three of us watched the street from my window with Avó's old opera glasses. Avó asked what we were doing.
"Birdwatching," I said, which was technically true.
At sunset we heard a buzz like a giant mosquito. A drone rose slowly from the roof of my building, turned over the street and flew past the windows, one by one, filming.
"A drone," whispered Inês. "If someone has a drone, they can photograph any window they want."
"Even a window on the second floor," I said.
Kiara didn't say anything. She was looking at the drone with her lips pressed together.
The next afternoon we found Josh in the café downstairs, eating his third pastel de nata. Rafa came too. He said that if there was a fight, we would need muscle. Rafa is the size of a coat stand.
"So you're the guy who flies the drone," said Rafa, sitting down without asking.
"Guilty," said Josh, smiling. "I'm a travel vlogger. I've filmed in forty countries. Want to see?"

He was from Newark, in New Jersey, from a neighbourhood called the Ironbound, where half the shops have Portuguese names. His grandparents had emigrated from a village near Aveiro before his dad was born. He spoke Portuguese like a robot that had learned it from his grandmother, which is exactly what had happened.
Inês asked him, very politely, when he had arrived in Portugal. He showed us his plane ticket on his phone. The second of January.
By the time Josh arrived in Portugal, the gull had already posted eleven times. Inês took out the marker and crossed him off the pizza box, which she had brought in her bag.
"So there's no fight?" said Rafa, disappointed.
"There's another pastel de nata," said Josh, and bought one for each of us.
Before we left, Josh gave me a link. "You make videos, right? Take my footage of your street. I've flown over it every evening this week. The light here is incredible."

That night I watched his footage frame by frame. I'm good at that. It's the only thing I'm better at than Inês. The drone flew over the beach, over the roofs, over the gulls, and then down our street at sunset, from a Thursday when we hadn't been watching.
At forty-seven seconds I pressed pause.

On the third floor of number 11, a window was open. Someone was holding an old photograph up in front of the street, as if they were comparing it with the real view, and they were taking a picture of it with a phone. I couldn't see a face. I could only see an arm, a phone, and the sleeve of a blue hoodie. When I zoomed in, I saw the tail of a big fish.
There are lots of fish hoodies in the world, I told myself. Thousands, probably. But only one of them lived on the third floor across the street from my window.

chapters.title: Wipeout
paragraphs: For a whole week I didn't say anything to Kiara. I didn't say anything to Inês either, which was worse, because Inês always knows when I'm hiding something. She says my ears go red. I watched the drone clip about two hundred times. The fish didn't change.

Then Coach Rui, who runs the school surf team, came to our class with a problem. The team was going to a Desporto Escolar surf competition in Ericeira, and he needed someone to film it for the school website.
"If you film us, you can come on the bus," he told me. "If you drop the camera in the sea, you'll walk home."

I said yes before he finished the sentence. Partly for the video. Mostly because of the fish. Inês couldn't come, because she had a chess tournament in Braga, so she made me promise to send her updates every two hours.

The bus left at six in the morning. By the time we arrived in Ericeira, I had eaten all my sandwiches, Coach Rui had sung four songs from the eighties, and a boy from 9.º had been sick in a plastic bag. Kiara sat at the front with the surf team and I sat at the back with the camera. We waved at each other once, like people in different countries.

Ericeira is a town of white houses with blue edges, narrow streets that all seem to go downhill, and a beach where fishermen still pull their boats up onto the sand. It is the first World Surfing Reserve in Europe, which is a fact Coach Rui told us six times before lunch. I sent Inês her first update: "Arrived. Sea big. Coach sings." She replied with a photo of a chessboard where she was clearly winning.

We stayed in a hostel which was run by Dona Graça, a tiny woman who had lived in Ericeira all her life. She said she had seen more surfers than seagulls. The hostel was full of people who had come from everywhere for the waves: two Germans in a van, a Brazilian family, and a group of Australians from Sydney who saw Kiara's board and started talking to her immediately. Dona Graça made fish soup for everyone that night. The Germans asked for the recipe, and she told them that if she gave them the recipe, she would have to kill them.

That evening I learned more about Australia than in all my years at school. The Australians talked about Bondi Beach and the volunteer lifesavers in red and yellow caps who watch the beaches every summer. Kiara talked about Perth. "If you take the ferry to Rottnest Island, you'll see quokkas," she told me. "They're little animals that look as if they're always smiling." One of the Australians, a quiet guy called Daniel, told me that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years before the first Europeans arrived, and that many towns and rivers still had Aboriginal names. He also told me that Uluru, the huge red rock in the middle of the country, is a sacred place for its traditional owners, and that tourists haven't been allowed to climb it since 2019.
"I've only seen it on a postcard," said Kiara. "Australia is enormous. If you drove from Perth to Sydney, it would take you about four days."

The next morning Coach Rui put me in a wetsuit which had belonged to someone much bigger and pushed me into the white water with a soft board. I fell off eleven times. I swallowed half the Atlantic. On my twelfth try I stood up for two seconds. For two seconds I was a surfer. Then I was a fish. My legs hurt in places where I didn't know I had legs. But that night I slept for nine hours without looking at my phone, which hasn't happened since I was about eight.
Kiara was watching from the sand. She clapped, and for a moment it was like before.
That night I couldn't stand it any more. I found her on the hostel terrace, looking at the lights of the fishing boats.
"Kiara, can I ask you something? Have you got another hoodie like the blue one? The fish one?"
"Why?"
I showed her the clip on my phone. I watched her face go pale and then red.
"So that's why you've been so weird all week," she said. "You think I'm the gull."
"I didn't say that."
"You don't need to. Everything strange started when the foreign girl arrived, so it must be the foreign girl. Rafa said exactly the same thing in October. Remember? You laughed at him."
"That isn't fair."
"No," she said. "It isn't." And she went inside.
I stayed on the terrace for a long time, feeling like the worst person in Ericeira. Only much later, on the bus home, did I realise something. She had never said it wasn't her.

At midnight Inês sent me a photo from her phone. She had gone to the school library before her tournament and had found a box of old school newspapers. It was a page from June 1979: "Two students from 9.º B have just finished a mural in the gym: a huge wave, eight metres long. The artists are Fátima Sousa and Lurdes Rocha."
Fátima Sousa. My grandmother.
Then another photo, a short note from 1995: "During the summer holidays the gym walls have been painted white."
"Painted twice," Inês wrote. "The wave is under the white paint, Tomás. And Fátima is your avó, isn't she?"

The final was the next morning. The waves had grown overnight, and the sea was dark and heavy. Kiara paddled out for the last heat. She caught a big wave, a beautiful one, and for a few seconds she flew. Then the lip came down on top of her and she disappeared.
Her board shot up into the air. Its leash had snapped. The board came in on the white water, alone, and landed on the sand a few metres from my feet.
I looked at the sea. I counted. Five seconds. Ten. Fifteen.
Kiara didn't come up.

glossary.pt: cabo (que prende a prancha ao pé)

chapters.title: Between the Flags
paragraphs: I dropped the camera. Coach Rui told me later that I dropped it on the sand, not in the sea, so I didn't have to walk home. I don't remember. I only remember running into the water in my jeans and my trainers, holding Kiara's broken board in front of me like a shield.

If I were a better swimmer, I would tell you that I saved her life. I didn't. A lifeguard called Marta did. She was on a jet ski before I had even reached the second wave. She pulled Kiara out of the water, laid her across the front of the jet ski and brought her in. I was standing in the sea up to my chest, holding a surfboard, completely useless.

Kiara had hit her head on the fin of her board. She was dizzy and there was blood on her forehead, but she was talking. The paramedics checked her in the medical tent and gave her three stitches. When they let me in, she was sitting on a stretcher, wrapped in a silver blanket like a baked potato.
"You came into the sea in jeans," she said.
"They're old jeans."

"In Australia you'd get a medal for that. Or a fine." She tried to smile. "At home, if you swim between the red and yellow flags, the lifesavers can see you. My uncle has been a volunteer lifesaver for twenty years. If he saw that wave, he'd be proud of me for about a second. Then he'd kill me."
Coach Rui came in, as white as the tent. "If I were your mum," he said, "I'd lock you in your room until you were thirty. Do you know what you did out there?"
"I caught the best wave of the day," said Kiara.
"You did," he admitted. "And then the wave caught you."
She didn't win the final. A girl from Peniche won. Kiara got a small trophy for the best wave of the competition, which she held all the way home like a teddy bear.

On the bus we sat together for the first time on the trip. She fell asleep after ten minutes with her head against the window. I looked at the stitches on her forehead and thought about her first day at our school, when everybody laughed at Rafa's kangaroo joke, and about all the questions she had answered since then. Spiders in shoes. Crocodiles. Koalas. Nobody had ever asked her what she missed. I hadn't asked either. Somewhere near Coimbra she woke up, saw me looking at her and said, "Stop observing me. For content." Then she went back to sleep.
I didn't tell Inês about the hoodie. I didn't tell anyone. I told myself that if I didn't say it out loud, it might not be true.

In March life went back to normal, or almost. Kiara came back to school with a plaster on her forehead and a new reputation. Rafa told everyone that she had fought a shark. By Friday the shark was six metres long and Kiara had punched it on the nose. Then on a rainy Tuesday Professora Lemos came into our classroom with a letter in her hand and a face that didn't say "Brilliant".

"I have news that some of you won't like," she said. "The town hall has finally approved the money for a new sports hall. The old gym, where your parents and grandparents played, is going to be knocked down in the first week of June."
Rafa cheered. "Good! I hate that gym. It smells of feet."
To be fair, the new hall sounded great. It would have solar panels on the roof, a climbing wall and showers that actually worked. Even I had to admit that.

Inês didn't cheer. She looked at me across the room, and I knew we were thinking the same thing. Behind the wall that was painted twice, the sea is waiting. Hurry up. Time is running out. The gull had known. Whoever the gull was, they had known about the gym before anyone.
That evening I sat with Avó Fátima while she was folding the washing. I had planned exactly what to say. In my head it sounded very clever.
"Avó, did you paint a wave in the school gym?"
She stopped folding. She held one of my socks in the air for a long time.
"Who told you that?"
"The school newspaper. June 1979. You and Lurdes Rocha. Eight metres long."

She put the sock down. "It was a long time ago. They painted over it. Everything gets painted over in the end, Tomás." Then she went to the kitchen and turned on the radio very loud, which in our house means that the conversation is closed.
Mum looked at me over her glasses. "What did you say to her?"
"I only asked about a painting."
"In this house," said Mum, "nothing is ever only a painting."
The next day Kiara sent Inês and me the same message: "Can you meet me at the statue after school? Please. Both of you. It's important."

We went. It was cold and windy, and the stone boy had a seagull on his head, which felt like a bad sign. Kiara was sitting on the wall with her school bag and an old shoebox on her knees. She didn't look like a detective any more. She looked like someone who had been awake all night.
"You were right in Ericeira," she said to me. "About the hoodie."
Inês looked at me. "What hoodie?"
Inês sat down next to her slowly, as if Kiara were a bomb.
"I'll explain everything," said Kiara. "But first I want you to see this. I should have shown you months ago."

She opened the shoebox. Inside there was an old photo album, and a notebook with a worn leather cover. On the first page of the album, under a plastic sheet, I saw a photo I already knew. Our school gate, in black and white, with the small trees and the toy cars.
Then she took out her phone, opened Instagram and turned the screen towards us. It was logged in to @gaivota_79.
"Hi," said Kiara. "I'm the gull."

chapters.title: Behind the Paint
paragraphs: For about ten seconds nobody said anything. The seagull on the statue's head said something, but nobody listened.
Inês spoke first. "You," she said. "You let me spend my Christmas holidays analysing reflections."
"I know."
"I made a spreadsheet, Kiara. With colours."
"I know. I'm sorry."
I didn't say anything. I was remembering the night of the window photo, the empty street, the curtains I had opened and closed until four in the morning.

Kiara opened the notebook with the leather cover. The pages were full of small, careful handwriting in English. "This is my grandma's," she said. "Lurdes Rocha. She's been ill for a year. The doctors say her memory is going to get worse. She forgets what she had for lunch and the names of her nurses. But she remembers 1979 perfectly. Every street. Every smell. Your grandmother, Tomás, is on almost every page."

She told us everything. Her grandmother had written the notebook in Perth, after the doctors had told her about her memory. She wanted to keep the important things safe on paper. When Kiara's mum got a job at the university in Porto, Grandma Lurdes asked them to look for a flat on her old street. By chance, her own old flat was free.

"When I arrived, I didn't know anybody," said Kiara. "People only talked to me to ask about kangaroos. Grandma's notebook talked about a box behind the wave, and about Fátima, and I couldn't find the wave, and I didn't know how to knock on your door and say: hi, my grandma was your grandma's best friend, can we break into the school gym together?"
"That's actually a normal sentence," said Inês.
"Not in my head. So I thought: if I make a mystery, everyone will want to solve it. And they'll help me find the box. And maybe..." She stopped.
"Maybe what?" I asked.
"Maybe they'll talk to me about something that isn't kangaroos."
"And the photo of my window?"
She looked at her shoes. "It was taken from my bedroom. I wanted you to be curious. I didn't think it would scare you. It was a really stupid thing to do."
"I couldn't sleep for a week."
"I know. I could see your light."
"That isn't helping, Kiara."

Inês laughed, and then she tried to stop laughing, and then I laughed too. It wasn't funny, exactly. It was just that I had imagined a ghost, a hacker and a criminal with a drone, and the gull had turned out to be a lonely girl with a shoebox.

We read the notebook together on the wall until it got dark. One page was about the mural: "The wave was painted in May and June 1979. The colours were mixed by hand, in yoghurt pots. A small box was hidden in the wall, behind the sun. It was locked with a little padlock. There were two keys."
"The box must still be there," said Inês. "They only painted over the wall. They didn't knock it down."
"It might be damaged," I said. "It's been forty-six years."
"It can't be completely destroyed. It's inside bricks."

On Monday Kiara did what Professora Lemos had told us in October. She told an adult. Actually, she told three: her mum, Professora Lemos and the head teacher, Diretor Amaral. I went with her. Inês came too, with her spreadsheet.
Diretor Amaral listened to the whole story without interrupting, which is unbelievable if you know him. Then he took off his glasses.
"The gym is going to be demolished on the third of June," he said. "The contract was signed in January. I'm sorry, but I can't let three students scratch the walls of a public building."
"What if an expert did it?" asked Professora Lemos.
He sighed. "If an expert tells me that the mural can be uncovered safely, I'll think about it. Think, not promise."

Two weeks later it was Earth Day, and the whole of 8.º B spent the morning cleaning Matosinhos beach. It was windy and grey. The sand was full of things that nobody wants to find: bottle caps, cigarette ends, pieces of fishing net, a single flip-flop, and plastic so old that the sun had turned it white. In two hours our class filled thirty-two bags.
"It's unbelievable how careless people are," said Inês, holding up a plastic fork with two fingers.
"In Perth we have Clean Up Australia Day," said Kiara. "Every March. My whole street used to go. Once we found a fridge on the beach."
"A fridge?"
"Nobody knows how. It's still a mystery."

Rafa refused to touch anything wet for the first hour. Then he found a glass bottle with a piece of paper inside it and became the happiest boy in Portugal. He opened it in front of everyone, very slowly. The message said: "Peixaria Silva. Fresh fish every day." It was an old advertisement. Rafa kept it anyway.

While we were walking back to school, Inês stopped in front of the old gym. "Building a new hall is good for the environment," she said. "Solar panels, rainwater, less energy. I get it. But it's a pity to destroy something beautiful just because nobody remembers it."
"Somebody remembers it," said Kiara.

That evening I decided to stop hiding things. I sat Avó Fátima down at the kitchen table and told her everything, from the first post to the shoebox. I told her that Lurdes lived in Perth, that she was ill, that her granddaughter lived across the street, and that her name was on almost every page of Lurdes's notebook.
Avó didn't drop anything this time. She sat very still with her hands on the table. When I finished, she got up without a word and went into her bedroom. I heard a drawer open and close.
She came back with a small, rusty key on a piece of faded blue string.

"There's a box behind the sun," she said. "We hid it together, Lurdes and I, on the last day of school in 1979. Two keys, one each. We promised to open it together when we were old." She put the key in my hand and closed my fingers around it. "I've kept this key for forty-six years. I've never wanted to use it."
"And now?"
"When are they knocking down the gym?"
"The third of June."
My grandmother looked at the calendar on the fridge. "Then you have six weeks," she said, "to bring me what's behind that wall."

chapters.title: The Sun on the Wall
paragraphs: Six weeks sounds like a long time. It isn't. It's thirty school days, and in May half of them are tests.

Professora Lemos helped us to write a letter to the Faculty of Fine Arts in Porto. Inês started a petition, which was signed by six hundred and twelve people in ten days, including Sr. Albano, who signed it twice. Inês made a graph of the signatures, obviously. Kiara posted on @gaivota_79 for the first time since Christmas, this time with her real name and her real face: "I'm Kiara. I'm the gull. I'm sorry for scaring people. Please help us save the wave." It was shared by more people than all my videos together.

A week later a journalist from the local newspaper came to interview us. The headline on Friday was: "Students try to save a forgotten wave". Avó cut it out and stuck it on the fridge, next to the calendar, and didn't say anything about it, which in Avó's language means she was very proud.

The day after that, an expert came to the school. Her name was Dr.ª Helena Matos and she restored old paintings for a living. She had grey hair cut very short, paint on her trainers and no patience for anyone who touched her tools.

She chose a small square at the bottom of the wall. The white paint was softened with a special gel and then removed very slowly with a scalpel, one millimetre at a time. We stood behind a line of yellow tape and didn't breathe. After forty minutes a little piece of colour appeared. It was blue. A deep, old, beautiful blue.
"Well," said Dr.ª Helena. "That must be your sea."

Meanwhile, we also had to prepare the end-of-year show. Every June, our school organises a show where each class performs something, and this year Professora Lemos had chosen the theme for 8.º B: "Many Voices: the English-speaking world".
"No fake accents," she warned us. "No costumes that make fun of people. I want you to show me something real. Brilliant."

Every group chose a country. Inês's group chose Canada and prepared a presentation about First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples, and about cities like Toronto, where people speak hundreds of languages. Inês also discovered that Canada has more lakes than any other country, and she told us every day for a week. Diogo's group chose New Zealand. They explained that Māori is one of the country's official languages, and they showed a video of the All Blacks performing the haka before a rugby match. Diogo's group practised the haka in the playground every break until Sr. Albano asked them to stop scaring the pigeons.

Rafa's group chose the Notting Hill Carnival in London, which was started by Caribbean communities. Rafa can't stand dancing, but after a long discussion he agreed to play the drums, and he turned out to be good at it, which annoyed him very much.

Kiara and I decided to make a video about Australia that wasn't about kangaroos. She interviewed her friends in Perth by video call. They spoke about their families, who came from Vietnam, Italy, India, Greece and Ireland. One of them was Aboriginal and talked about his grandmother's language. Her friend Minh said that people always asked him where he was really from. "Perth," he said, looking straight into the camera. "I'm really from Perth." Kiara called the video "Not Everyone Surfs".
"But you surf," I said.
"I know. It's ironic. Australians love irony."

Every afternoon after school we ran to the gym to watch the restoration. The restorers couldn't uncover the whole wall in time. It was impossible. But Dr.ª Helena chose the most important part, and every day a bit more was revealed: the curve of a huge wave, white foam, a strip of yellow sand. Then two small figures appeared on top of the wave, standing on one surfboard together. One girl had dark plaits.
"That has to be your grandmother," said Kiara.
"It can't be anyone else. Look at her face. She's telling the wave what to do."

On the fifteenth day the sun appeared in the top corner of the mural, round, orange and slightly crooked. Inês grabbed my arm. "Behind the sun," she whispered. "Exactly like the notebook." Dr.ª Helena tapped the sun with her finger, and it made a hollow sound.
"Interesting," she said. "This part isn't painted on the wall. It's painted on a wooden board, and the board is screwed into the bricks."

Diretor Amaral had to give permission to remove it. He stood in front of the mural for a long time with his hands in his pockets. Then he said, "Do it. Carefully." I think the wave had uncovered something in him too.

We called Avó Fátima. She came to the school that afternoon. She had refused to come inside the building for decades. She walked through the gate slowly, past the stone boy, past Sr. Albano, who took off his cap, and into the old gym. When she saw the wave, she stopped walking.
"We spilt yellow paint there," she said quietly, pointing at the sand. "Lurdes slipped on it and sat in it. She had a yellow bottom for a week."

Dr.ª Helena put on white gloves. The four screws were old and stiff. Dr.ª Helena removed them one by one, and the board was lifted off the wall. Behind it there was a hole in the bricks, and in the hole there was a rectangular biscuit tin, rusty at the corners, with a tiny padlock on the front.
Avó took the key from her pocket. Her hands were shaking, so she gave it to me. I put it into the padlock and turned. It didn't move. I tried again, gently. There was a small click.

Inside there were two friendship bracelets, blue and white, a cassette tape with "Summer 1979" written on it, a photo of two girls with paint on their faces, and something that Avó Fátima didn't expect.
On top of everything there was an envelope. Someone had written on it in blue ink: "Para a Fátima. Lê isto antes de me odiares." For Fátima. Read this before you hate me.
Avó stared at it. Her face had gone completely white.
"This wasn't here," she whispered. "When we closed the box in 1979, there was no letter."

chapters.title: The Same Wave
paragraphs: Avó Fátima didn't open the envelope in the gym. She held it against her chest all the way home, as if someone might steal it. At home she sat in her armchair by the window, opened it with a knife and read it. Then she read it again. Then she gave it to me.
"Read it to me," she said. "Out loud. My glasses are wrong."
Her glasses were fine. I read it anyway. It was written in Portuguese, in a round, teenage handwriting. This is my translation, and I promise it is as good as I could make it.

"Fátima, my father told me last night that we are leaving for Australia on Saturday. He has found a job there. I tried to tell you on Thursday, at the beach, and I couldn't. I know that if I say goodbye to you, I won't be able to get on the plane. So I'm a coward and I'm writing a letter. I'm putting it in our box with my key, because you are the only person in the world who can open it now. I'll wait for your letter. I'll wait for as long as it takes. Your friend forever, L."

Under the letter there was an address in Perth. At the bottom of the tin, under the photo, there was a second rusty key on a piece of faded pink string. Lurdes had left her key with her friend, as she had promised.
Avó looked out of the window at the building across the street for a long time.

"She put it in the box after school had finished," she said. "She must have climbed in through the gym window. She was always good at climbing." Her voice was steady, but her eyes weren't. "And I never opened the box. I was too angry. I thought she had left without a word. And she was waiting for a letter that I never wrote."
"For forty-six years," I said.
"Don't do maths at me, Tomás."

The gym was demolished on the third of June, as planned. Before that, the whole mural was photographed in high resolution by Dr.ª Helena's team, and the wooden sun was carefully removed and taken to the Faculty of Fine Arts. Diretor Amaral announced that next year the wave will be painted again on a wall of the new sports hall, by students, with Dr.ª Helena's help. When we heard that, Rafa offered to paint the seagulls. Nobody was surprised that he wanted to paint them very small.

The end-of-year show was on a Friday evening in June. The school hall was full and hot. Parents were fanning themselves with the programme, and little brothers were crawling under the chairs. Inês's group was brilliant. Diogo's haka made a grandmother in the front row stand up and clap. Rafa played the drums with his eyes closed and didn't miss a beat, and for the first time in his life he didn't check how many people were filming him.

Our video was the last thing on the programme. My hands were sweating so much that I almost dropped the remote control. Before I made it, I did something I had never done before. I asked every single person who appeared in it if they were happy to be in it. Inês said yes. Kiara said yes. Avó Fátima said, "Only from my good side," and then she said she didn't have a bad side.

The video told the whole story, from the account with no face to the biscuit tin. When it finished, the hall was silent. Then Professora Lemos, who had promised to say nothing, stood up and said, "Brilliant." Nobody laughed. For once she meant it completely.
But the real show started after the applause.

It was nine o'clock in Matosinhos, which meant it was four in the morning in Perth. Kiara had arranged everything with her aunt. The big screen at the back of the stage flickered, and then there was a kitchen, a kettle, a window full of darkness, and an old woman in a pink dressing gown, sitting very straight.
Kiara took Avó Fátima's hand and led her onto the stage. My grandmother is not someone who likes being looked at. But she walked up there in front of three hundred people as if she did it every day.
At first Lurdes didn't seem to understand. She looked at the screen politely, the way you look at a stranger. Kiara's aunt whispered something to her. Nothing happened.
Then Avó Fátima took a blue and white bracelet out of her pocket and held it up to the camera.
Lurdes leaned forward. She looked for a long time. Then she smiled, and her whole face changed.
"Fátima," she said. "You've got old."
"So have you," said my grandmother.

The hall exploded with laughter, and half of it was crying at the same time. Then Lurdes started speaking in Portuguese, an old Matosinhos Portuguese that nobody uses any more, and Avó answered her, and for a few minutes three hundred people sat in a hot school hall and watched two girls from 1979 talk about yellow paint. Kiara was standing next to me, crying and laughing, and holding my arm so hard that I had bruises the next day.
I had my camera in my hand the whole time. I didn't press record. It was the best video I have never made.

On the last day of term, @gaivota_79 posted for the last time. It was a photo of the stone boy with five of us sitting around him: Inês, Rafa, Kiara, me and, in the middle, Avó Fátima, who had refused to smile and then smiled anyway. The caption said: "The gull has landed. Thank you, 8.º B." The next day Kiara deleted the account. She didn't need a mask any more.

In July I finally caught a real wave. It was small and it was slow, and Kiara was shouting instructions at me the whole time, but I stood up and I stayed up all the way to the sand. Inês filmed it from the beach, between two games of chess against herself. She says she won both.
When I came out of the water, I sat down to eat my sandwich. A seagull landed next to me, looked me straight in the eye, took the whole sandwich and flew away.
Some mysteries are solved. Some seagulls are just seagulls.

reading.title: The Account with No Face
text: My name is Tomás Ferreira. I'm thirteen, I live in Matosinhos, and I have made forty-three videos for my YouTube channel. The channel has got forty-one subscribers. Twelve of them are relatives.

On the first day of 8.º ano I walked to school with Inês Carvalho. She has been my best friend since nursery. In that time she has beaten me at chess more than three hundred times. I have beaten her once.

In our English lesson, Professora Lemos introduced a new girl. "This is Kiara Walsh. She has just arrived from Perth, in Australia." Rafa put his hand up. "So you've got a pet kangaroo, haven't you?" Kiara looked at him calmly. "No. Have you got a pet sardine?" The whole class laughed, and they weren't laughing with Rafa.

At break, Kiara told us that her grandmother was born in Matosinhos. "She went to this school, actually. A long time ago." After school we found out that Kiara lived in the building opposite mine. She looked up at my building for a long time. Then she smiled in a way I didn't understand.

That evening our class group chat exploded. A strange account called @gaivota_79 had followed everyone in 8.º B. It had no profile picture, only a drawing of a seagull. Its first post was an old black-and-white photo of our school gate, from 1979. The caption said: "I've been away for a long time. Have you missed me? Clue 1: Look for the boy who has never lost a game."
Inês wrote in the chat: "Don't click on any links. Don't follow it back."

At 23:47 there was a new post: an old photo of my building, with a girl at my window. The caption said: "You've lived here all your life, haven't you, Tomás?" I went to the window. The street was empty. On the railing of my balcony, a huge seagull was staring at me.
reading.source: Adapted from The Gull Who Knew My Name, Chapter 1

fichas.focus: Reading: Chapter 2 · Grammar: present perfect vs past simple, phrasal verbs, question tags

reading.title: Don't Feed the Gull
text: The next morning I showed the photo to Mum. "Have you replied to it?" she asked. "No." "Have you clicked on anything?" "No. I've only looked at it. A lot." "Good. Don't answer it and don't delete anything. We're going to report it."

At school, Professora Lemos turned her English lesson into an online safety lesson. "Has anyone here ever accepted a follow request from a stranger?" she asked. About twenty hands went up. Rafa's went up first. "I've accepted everyone," he said proudly. "More followers." "And how many of those followers have you actually met?" Rafa started counting on his fingers. Then he stopped.

"The rule is simple," she said. "If something online makes you feel scared, you tell an adult you trust. You report it. You never share your address. And you don't feed the gull. Attention is what it wants, isn't it?"

At lunch, Inês looked at the clue again: Look for the boy who has never lost a game. "Who has never lost a game?" she asked. "Someone who has never played one," said Kiara quietly. In the school garden there is a small stone statue of a boy with a ball under his arm. He has stood there for about fifty years.

After school we looked around the statue. I was ready to give up when Kiara brushed the moss off the back of the stone. Someone had scratched letters into it: L + F 1979. AMIGAS PARA SEMPRE. "Friends forever," Kiara translated softly.

That night I showed Avó Fátima the photo of the letters. "Avó, you were at the school in 1979, weren't you?" She looked at the screen and dropped her plate. My grandmother has never dropped anything in her life. She went into her bedroom and closed the door, and for the first time in my life I heard her cry.
reading.source: Adapted from The Gull Who Knew My Name, Chapter 2

reading.title: Take It Down
text: I made a video called The Gull Mystery: What We've Found So Far. It had dramatic music and a beautiful shot of Inês in the school garden. I uploaded it on a Friday night without asking her. By Saturday morning it had two thousand views. My channel has never had so many views.

On Monday, at the school Magusto, Inês didn't say hello. "You've put my face on the internet," she said. "Without asking me. You've shown everyone our school. You've shown the gull exactly what we know. Take it down." Then she walked away.

I took the video down that night, but it didn't help. I have known Inês for ten years and we have never had a real fight. It turned out that a real fight feels like a stomach ache that slowly moves up into your chest.

Kiara sat with me during those weeks. She was homesick. "At home Christmas is in summer," she said. "We go to the beach and have a barbecue. Then Dad falls asleep in the sun and gets burnt. Every year!" Then she asked, "Have you said sorry to Inês?" "I've taken the video down." "That isn't what I asked, is it?"

On Saturday I knocked on Inês's door with her favourite chocolate and my chess set. "I was wrong," I said. "I only thought about the views. I'm sorry." She took the chocolate. "White or black?" she said. That's how Inês says "I forgive you".
On Christmas Eve, Avó Fátima told me that L was Lurdes, her best friend. In 1980 Lurdes's family emigrated, and she left without saying goodbye. They have never spoken since then.

On Boxing Day Inês called me. "I've found out something. In the gull's last photo there's a reflection of a window with green railings. Railings like that only exist on one street in Matosinhos. Tomás, the gull lives on your street."

text: In January, Inês, Kiara and I made a list of everyone who lived on our street. Number 8: Dona Rosário, who feeds every cat in Matosinhos. Number 10: Sr. Pinto, whose dog barks at buses. Number 12, first floor: an Airbnb, which is always full of tourists. Number 11, third floor: Kiara.
Inês explained her theory. "If you take a photo of a glossy photo, the light makes a reflection. If there's a reflection, there's a window. And if the window has green railings, it's on this street."

That week the Airbnb had three guests. Mr and Mrs Medeiros were a retired couple from Toronto, whose parents had left the Azores for Canada in the 1960s. They asked me how to get to Livraria Lello. "If you take the metro, you'll be there in half an hour," I said. "But you'll queue for an hour." They told me that their grandchildren speak English at home and learn French at school, because Canada has two official languages.

The third guest was Josh, an American with a beard and a drone. On Saturday evening we saw his drone fly past the windows of our street, filming. "If someone has a drone, they can photograph any window," whispered Inês.

The next day we found Josh in the café. He was a travel vlogger from Newark, New Jersey, from a neighbourhood where half the shops have Portuguese names. His grandparents had emigrated from a village near Aveiro before his dad was born. He showed us his plane ticket: he had arrived on the second of January. By then, the gull had already posted eleven times. Josh couldn't be the gull.

That night I watched Josh's drone footage frame by frame. At forty-seven seconds I pressed pause. On the third floor of number 11, someone was holding an old photograph in front of the window and taking a picture of it with a phone. I couldn't see a face. I could only see the sleeve of a blue hoodie, with the tail of a big fish on it.

text: Coach Rui, who runs the school surf team, needed someone to film a competition in Ericeira. "If you film us, you can come on the bus," he told me. I said yes before he finished the sentence.

By the time we arrived in Ericeira, I had eaten all my sandwiches and a boy from 9.º had been sick in a plastic bag. Ericeira is a town of white houses with blue edges, and it is the first World Surfing Reserve in Europe. We stayed in a hostel which was run by Dona Graça, a tiny woman who had lived there all her life.

The hostel was full of people who had come for the waves, including a group of Australians. One of them, Daniel, told me that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years before the first Europeans arrived. Kiara laughed when I looked at a map. "Australia is enormous. If you drove from Perth to Sydney, it would take you about four days."
The next morning I had my first surf lesson. I fell off eleven times. On my twelfth try I stood up for two seconds. For two seconds I was a surfer.

That night I showed Kiara the drone clip. Her face went pale and then red. "You think I'm the gull," she said. "Everything strange started when the foreign girl arrived, so it must be the foreign girl." She went inside. Much later I realised that she had never said it wasn't her.

At midnight Inês sent me a page from an old school newspaper which she had found in the library. It was from June 1979: "Two students have just finished a mural in the gym: a huge wave. The artists are Fátima Sousa and Lurdes Rocha." Fátima Sousa. My grandmother.

The next morning Kiara paddled out for the final. She caught a big wave, and then the wave came down on top of her. Her board came back to the beach alone. I counted. Five seconds. Ten. Fifteen. Kiara didn't come up.

text: I ran into the water in my jeans and trainers. If I were a better swimmer, I would tell you that I saved Kiara's life. I didn't. A lifeguard called Marta did. She pulled Kiara out of the water and brought her in on a jet ski.

Kiara had hit her head on the fin of her board. The paramedics gave her three stitches. "You came into the sea in jeans," she said. "At home, if you swim between the red and yellow flags, the lifesavers can see you. My uncle has been a volunteer lifesaver for twenty years. If he saw that wave, he'd be proud of me for about a second. Then he'd kill me."
Coach Rui was as white as the tent. "If I were your mum, I'd lock you in your room until you were thirty."
On the bus home, Kiara fell asleep. I thought about all the questions she had answered since September: spiders, crocodiles, koalas. Nobody had ever asked her what she missed.

In March, Professora Lemos gave us some news. "The old gym, where your parents and grandparents played, is going to be knocked down in June." Rafa cheered. Inês looked at me. Behind the wall that was painted twice, the sea is waiting. The gull had known about the gym before anyone.

That evening I asked Avó Fátima, "Did you paint a wave in the school gym?" She stopped folding the washing. "It was a long time ago. They painted over it. Everything gets painted over in the end, Tomás."

The next day Kiara asked Inês and me to meet her at the statue. She had an old shoebox with a photo album and a notebook. Then she took out her phone and turned the screen towards us. It was logged in to @gaivota_79. "Hi," she said. "I'm the gull."

reading.title: Behind the Paint
text: Kiara opened her grandmother's notebook. "Grandma Lurdes wrote this in Perth," she said. "She's ill, and the doctors say her memory is going to get worse. But she remembers 1979 perfectly. Your grandmother, Tomás, is on almost every page."

Kiara explained that she didn't know anybody when she arrived. "People only talked to me to ask about kangaroos. So I thought: if I make a mystery, everyone will want to solve it, and they'll help me find the box." And the photo of my window? "It was taken from my bedroom. I didn't think it would scare you. It was a really stupid thing to do."

One page of the notebook was about the mural: "The wave was painted in May and June 1979. The colours were mixed by hand. A small box was hidden in the wall, behind the sun. It was locked with a little padlock. There were two keys."
"The box must still be there," said Inês. "They only painted over the wall." "It might be damaged," I said. "It can't be completely destroyed. It's inside bricks."

Kiara decided to tell the adults. Diretor Amaral listened to the whole story. "The gym is going to be demolished on the third of June," he said. "The contract was signed in January. If an expert tells me that the mural can be uncovered safely, I'll think about it."

On Earth Day our class spent the morning cleaning Matosinhos beach. We found bottle caps, cigarette ends and pieces of fishing net. "It's unbelievable how careless people are," said Inês. Rafa refused to touch anything wet for the first hour. Then he found a bottle with a message inside. It was an old advertisement for a fish shop.

That evening I told Avó Fátima everything. She went to her bedroom and came back with a small rusty key. "We hid a box behind the sun, Lurdes and I. Two keys, one each. I've kept this key for forty-six years." She looked at the calendar. "You have six weeks to bring me what's behind that wall."

text: Six weeks sounds like a long time. It isn't. Inês started a petition, which was signed by six hundred and twelve people in ten days. Kiara posted on @gaivota_79 again, this time with her real name and her real face: "I'm Kiara. I'm the gull. I'm sorry for scaring people. Please help us save the wave."

An expert came to the school. Dr.ª Helena Matos restored old paintings for a living. The white paint was softened with a special gel and removed very slowly with a scalpel. After forty minutes a little piece of deep blue appeared. "Well," she said. "That must be your sea."

Meanwhile, we had to prepare the end-of-year show. The theme was "Many Voices: the English-speaking world". "No fake accents," said Professora Lemos. "No costumes that make fun of people." Inês's group chose Canada and talked about First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples. Diogo's group explained that Māori is an official language of New Zealand. Rafa can't stand dancing, but he agreed to play the drums. Kiara and I made a video called "Not Everyone Surfs", about Australians whose families came from Vietnam, Italy, India and Greece.

Every day a bit more of the mural was revealed: a huge wave, white foam and two girls on one surfboard. One girl had dark plaits. Then the sun appeared in the corner. It wasn't painted on the wall. It was painted on a wooden board. The board was removed, and behind it, in a hole in the bricks, there was a rusty biscuit tin.

Avó Fátima came to the school for the first time in decades. I turned her key in the padlock. Inside there were two friendship bracelets, a cassette tape and a photo of two girls with paint on their faces. On top there was an envelope: "For Fátima. Read this before you hate me." Avó's face went white. "This wasn't here," she whispered. "When we closed the box in 1979, there was no letter."

fichas.title: The Same Wave
fichas.focus: Reading: Chapter 9 · Grammar: word formation, modal verbs of deduction, passive voice, gerund and infinitive

reading.title: The Same Wave
text: At home Avó Fátima opened the envelope and asked me to read it to her. It was written in Portuguese, in a round teenage handwriting. "Fátima, my father told me last night that we are leaving for Australia on Saturday. I tried to tell you on Thursday, and I couldn't. If I say goodbye to you, I won't be able to get on the plane. So I'm a coward and I'm writing a letter. I'm putting it in our box with my key. I'll wait for your letter. Your friend forever, L."

At the bottom of the tin there was a second rusty key. Avó looked out of the window for a long time. "She must have climbed in through the gym window," she said. "And I never opened the box. I was too angry. She was waiting for a letter that I never wrote."
The gym was demolished on the third of June. Before that, the whole mural was photographed by Dr.ª Helena's team. Next year the wave will be painted again on a wall of the new sports hall.

The end-of-year show was on a Friday evening. Before the show, I asked everyone in our video if they were happy to appear in it. When the video finished, Professora Lemos stood up and said, "Brilliant." For once she meant it completely.

It was nine o'clock in Matosinhos and four in the morning in Perth. The big screen showed a kitchen and an old woman in a pink dressing gown. At first Lurdes didn't seem to recognise anyone. Then Avó Fátima held up a blue and white friendship bracelet. Lurdes leaned forward and smiled. "Fátima," she said. "You've got old." "So have you," said my grandmother. The whole hall laughed and cried at the same time.
I had my camera in my hand the whole time. I didn't press record. It was the best video I have never made.
In July I finally caught a real wave. When I came out of the water, a seagull took my sandwich and flew away. Some mysteries are solved. Some seagulls are just seagulls.
reading.source: Adapted from The Gull Who Knew My Name, Chapter 9

she hasn't worked		Have you worked?

Use

UseKey wordsExamples
Life experience – something that happened at some time in your life (we don't say when)ever (questions)
never (negative)

Position of the key words

WordPositionExample
ever, never, just, alreadybetween have / has and the past participleHave you ever tried? · I've just seen her. · He's already gone.
yetat the end of negative sentences and questionsI haven't eaten yet. · Has it started yet?
