For + a period of time: for two hours, for a week, for ages, for a long time. Since + the moment it started: since Monday, since 2020, since I was a child, since lunchtime. I've had this phone for a year = since last October.
Been vs gone: has been to = went and came back; has gone to = is still there. Ana has been to Paris twice. (She's home now.) · Ana has gone to Paris. (She's in Paris now.)

sebenta.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
sebenta.html:
Present Perfect – have / has + past participlePast Simple – -ed / 2nd column
The time is not mentioned or is not finished (today, this week, ever, so far).The time is finished and often mentioned (yesterday, last year, in 2010, two days ago, when I was ten).
Connection with the present: result, news, experience, situation that continues.The action is completed and belongs to the past; no connection with now.
I've visited Spain three times. (in my life)
She's broken her leg. (it's broken now)
I've known him for years. (I still know him)
Have you seen Tom today?		I visited Spain last summer.
She broke her leg in March.
I knew him when I was at school.
Did you see Tom yesterday?

Typical markers

Present PerfectPast Simple
ever, never, just, already, yet, still, for, since, so far, recently, lately, today, this week, how long…?yesterday, last night / week / year, … ago, in 2015, on Monday, at 6 o'clock, when…?, then, the other day

Conversations: start general, then give details

We often begin with the present perfect (experience, no time) and continue with the past simple to give details (when, where, with whom):

"Have you ever been to a concert?" "Yes, I have. I went to one last month." "Who did you see?" "I saw Coldplay. It was amazing!"
I've read that book. I read it when I was twelve and I loved it.

Questions with How long…? and When…?

QuestionAnswer
How long have you lived here? (still true)(I've lived here) for five years / since 2021.
When did you move here? (finished action)(I moved here) in 2021 / five years ago.
How long did you live in Porto? (finished)(I lived there) for two years. (not any more)
Typical mistakes: I have seen him yesterday → I saw him yesterday. · I live here since 2015 → I have lived here since 2015. · Did you ever go to Italy? → Have you ever been to Italy? · I didn't finish yet → I haven't finished yet. · She has gone to Rome last year → She went to Rome last year.

Summary

QuestionPresent PerfectPast Simple
Do we say when?No (or unfinished time)Yes (or it is understood)
Is the time finished?No – it continues or is "up to now"Yes
Connection with now?Yes (result, experience, still true)No
Typical questionsHave you ever…? How long…? …yet?When…? What time…? How long ago…?

sebenta.title: Past Perfect
sebenta.html:
Form

AffirmativeNegativeQuestionShort answers
subject + had ('d) + past participle
I had left. · She'd gone.		hadn't + past participle
They hadn't seen it.		Had + subject + past participle?
Had he finished?		Yes, he had.
No, he hadn't.

The same form for all persons. Careful with 'd: I'd gone = I had gone (past perfect); I'd go = I would go.

Use: "the past of the past"

The past perfect shows that one action happened before another action or moment in the past. The earlier action takes the past perfect; the later one takes the past simple.

Earlier action (past perfect)Order of events
When I arrived, the film had already started.The film started → then I arrived.
She had never flown before that day.Her first flight was that day.
By the time we got there, they had sold all the tickets.The tickets were sold → then we got there.
He was tired because he hadn't slept well.The bad night came first.

Typical words with the past perfect

already · just · never · before · after · by the time · when · until · because. After she had finished work, she went home. · I didn't know who he was – I had never met him before.

Past Simple → Past Perfect changes the order:
When I got home, my mum cooked dinner.
(I arrived first, then she cooked.)
When I got home, my mum had cooked dinner.
(Dinner was ready before I arrived.)
Present Perfect vs Past Perfect:
I've lost my keys. (before now)
I had lost my keys, so I couldn't get in. (before a past moment)
Present perfect = have / has; past perfect = had.
No past perfect is needed when the actions happen in order with and, then, after that: She opened the door and went in. Use it when you want to make clear that something happened earlier: When she opened the door, she saw that someone had broken the window.

Past perfect in stories

Stories are usually told in the past simple; the past perfect is used to go back and explain what had happened before: Tom looked at his phone and smiled. Ana had sent him a message – she had passed her exam!

Overview: perfect tenses

TenseFormMeaning
Present Perfecthave / has + past participlebefore now; result or experience up to now
Past Perfecthad + past participlebefore another moment in the past

sebenta.title: Conditionals: type 0, 1 and 2
sebenta.html:
TypeFormUseExample
ZeroIf + present simple,
present simple		facts, general truths, things that always happen (if = when)If you heat ice, it melts.
If I don't sleep enough, I feel tired.
FirstIf + present simple,
will / won't + verb		real possibility in the present or future; promises, warningsIf it rains, we'll stay at home.
If you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.
SecondIf + past simple,
would / wouldn't + verb		unreal, imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future; adviceIf I had a million euros, I would travel the world.
If I were you, I'd tell the truth.

Notes

  • The if-clause can come first or second. With the if-clause first, use a comma: If I see her, I'll tell her. / I'll tell her if I see her.
  • Never use will or would in the if-clause: If it will rain → If it rains… · If I would have → If I had…
  • In the second conditional, were is used for all persons, especially in If I were you: If she were here, she'd help us.
  • Other modals can replace will / would: can, may, might, should, could. If you finish early, you can go. · If I had a car, I could drive you.
  • Imperatives in the first conditional: If you see Tom, tell him to call me.
  • Unless = if … not: I won't go unless you come too. = I won't go if you don't come.
  • Other words like if in the first conditional: when, as soon as, as long as, in case. I'll call you when I arrive. · Take a coat in case it gets cold.

First or second conditional?

First – real / possibleSecond – unreal / imaginary
If I pass the exam, my parents will be happy. (possible – I'm studying)If I passed without studying, my parents would be surprised. (unlikely)
If it's sunny tomorrow, we'll go to the beach.If I lived by the sea, I'd go to the beach every day. (I don't live there)
What will you do if you win?What would you do if you won the lottery?

The difference is not time but how real the speaker thinks the situation is. Both can refer to the future.

Overview of conditionals

TypeIf-clauseMain clauseTime / reality
Zeropresent simplepresent simplealways true
Firstpresent simplewill + verbpresent / future, real or possible
Secondpast simplewould + verbpresent / future, unreal or unlikely
Typical mistakes: If I will see him → If I see him… · If I would be you → If I were you… · If I have money I would buy it → If I had money, I would buy it. · I'll go if it won't rain → I'll go if it doesn't rain.

sebenta.title: Relative pronouns and defining relative clauses
sebenta.html:
A relative clause gives information about a noun. It starts with a relative pronoun and joins two sentences into one: This is the boy. He won the race. → This is the boy who won the race.

PronounRefers toExamples
whopeoplethe man who lives next door · a doctor is someone who treats sick people
whichthings, animalsthe book which I'm reading · a dog is an animal which barks
thatpeople, things or animals (informal; can replace who / which)the car that I bought · the girl that sits next to me
whosepossession (= his / her / their / its)the girl whose phone was stolen · a friend whose dad is a pilot
whereplacesthe town where I was born · a library is a place where you borrow books
whentimethe day when we met · 2020 was the year when everything changed
whyreason (after the reason)the reason why he left

Defining relative clauses

They give essential information: without the clause we don't know which person or thing we are talking about. No commas. The girl who is wearing a red jacket is my cousin. (which girl? the one in the red jacket)

Subject or object?

Pronoun = subject of the clause (verb follows)Pronoun = object of the clause (subject follows)
The woman who called is my aunt.
I like films which make me laugh.		The woman (who) you met is my aunt.
I like the film (which) we saw yesterday.
The pronoun cannot be left out.The pronoun can be left out (very common in speech).
Do not repeat the subject or object: the man who he lives next door → the man who lives next door · the book which I bought it → the book which I bought. Whose, where and when cannot be left out: the house where I grew up.

Defining people, things and places

Relative clauses are very useful for definitions and describing:

  • A vet is a person who looks after animals. · A vegetarian is someone who doesn't eat meat.
  • A smartphone is a device which / that you use to go online. · Recycling is something that everyone should do.
  • A stadium is a place where people watch sports. · Christmas is a time when families get together.

Joining sentences

Two sentencesOne sentence with a relative clause
I have a friend. She speaks four languages.I have a friend who speaks four languages.
That's the hotel. We stayed there last year.That's the hotel where we stayed last year.
He is the singer. His new song is number one.He is the singer whose new song is number one.

sebenta.title: The passive voice
sebenta.html:
In an active sentence the subject does the action: Shakespeare wrote Hamlet. In a passive sentence the subject receives the action: Hamlet was written by Shakespeare. We use the passive when the action or the result is more important than who did it, or when we don't know who did it.

Form: be + past participle

TenseActivePassive
Present Simple
am / is / are + p.p.		They clean the rooms every day.
People speak English here.		The rooms are cleaned every day.
English is spoken here.
Past Simple
was / were + p.p.		They built the bridge in 1966.
Someone stole my bike.		The bridge was built in 1966.
My bike was stolen.

How to change active into passive

  1. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive. They make these cars in Japan. → These cars …
  2. Put the verb be in the same tense as the active verb (make → present simple → are). These cars are …
  3. Add the past participle (p. 14). These cars are made in Japan.
  4. Add by + agent only if it is important or new information. The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci.
NegativeQuestionsWh- questions
The letter wasn't sent.
Dogs aren't allowed here.		Is breakfast included?
Were the tickets sold?		When was the castle built?
Where are these phones made?

When to leave out the agent (by…)

ReasonExample
We don't know who did itMy wallet was stolen yesterday.
It is obvious or not importantThe thief was arrested. (by the police, obviously) · Rice is grown in Asia.
"People in general" (people, they, someone)Portuguese is spoken in Brazil. (not by people)

Passive with other tenses (a first look)

TenseActivePassive
Present ContinuousThey are repairing the road.The road is being repaired.
Present PerfectSomeone has found my bag.My bag has been found.
Future (will)They will open the museum in May.The museum will be opened in May.
Modal verbsYou must wear a helmet.A helmet must be worn.
Typical uses: processes and facts (Paper is made from wood), news (Two men were injured in the accident), rules and signs (Photos are not allowed), history (America was discovered in 1492).
Typical mistakes: The film was direct by → was directed by (past participle!) · English speaks here → English is spoken here · The book written by → The book was written by (never forget be) · These shoes was made → These shoes were made (agree with the subject).

sebenta.title: Modal verbs: deduction and possibility
sebenta.html:
Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would) are followed by the bare infinitive (no to), have no -s in the 3rd person and form negatives and questions without do: She might come. · Can he swim? · You mustn't touch it.

Deduction: how sure are you?

CertaintyModal + verbExamples
Sure it is true (≈ 95%)must + verbThe lights are on – they must be at home.
She's got three dogs – she must love animals.
Possible (≈ 50%) – perhaps, maybemay / might / could + verbHe might be in the library. · It may rain later.
That could be Ana's bag – she has one like it.
Sure it is NOT true (≈ 95%)can't + verbThat can't be Ana – she's in Paris.
He can't know the answer; he wasn't in class.
The opposite of must (deduction) is can't, not mustn't: It must be true. / It can't be true. Mustn't = prohibition (You mustn't run in the corridor). In negative sentences of possibility use may not / might not: She might not come. (could not = past ability).

With continuous verbs

must / might / can't + be + -ing for actions in progress: He isn't answering – he must be sleeping. · They might be having lunch. · She can't be working; it's Sunday.

Possibility and probability in the future

MeaningExamples
will – certainIt will be cold in January.
may / might / could – possibleWe might go camping this summer. · It could snow tonight.
won't – certainly notShe won't be late – she never is.

Other modals: a reminder from the 7th grade

FunctionModalsExamples
Abilitycan / can't (present), could / couldn't (past), be able toI can swim. · She could read at four.
Permission / requestscan, could (polite), may (formal)Can I go out? · Could you help me? · May I come in?
Obligationmust (the speaker decides), have to (a rule)I must study. · We have to wear a uniform.
Prohibitionmustn't, can'tYou mustn't use your phone in class.
No obligationdon't have to, needn'tYou don't have to come. (it isn't necessary)
Adviceshould / shouldn't, ought toYou should see a doctor. · You shouldn't share your password.
mustn't = it is forbidden (You mustn't smoke here) ≠ don't have to = it isn't necessary (You don't have to pay). Past of must / have to = had to: I had to stay at home yesterday.

sebenta.title: Question tags
sebenta.html:
A question tag is a short question at the end of a sentence. We use it to check information or to ask for agreement: It's cold today, isn't it?

The rule

Positive sentence → negative tag · Negative sentence → positive tag. The tag uses the same auxiliary (or modal) as the sentence and a pronoun. You are Portuguese, aren't you? · She doesn't like fish, does she?
Verb in the sentenceTagExamples
be (am / is / are / was / were)same form of beHe's your brother, isn't he? · They weren't at school, were they?
You're tired, aren't you? · It was fun, wasn't it?
present simple (no auxiliary)do / doesYou like pizza, don't you? · She lives in Faro, doesn't she?
They don't know, do they?
past simple (no auxiliary)didYou went to the party, didn't you? · He didn't call, did he?
present perfect (have / has)have / hasYou've finished, haven't you? · She hasn't been here, has she?
past perfect (had)hadThey had left, hadn't they?
will / won'twill / won'tYou'll help me, won't you? · It won't hurt, will it?
can / could / must / should / wouldsame modalShe can drive, can't she? · We should go, shouldn't we?
He couldn't come, could he?

Special cases

SentenceTag
I am …aren't I? I'm late, aren't I?
Let's …shall we? Let's go, shall we?
Imperative (Open the door)will you? / can you? Close the window, will you?
Negative imperative (Don't …)will you? Don't be late, will you?
There is / areisn't / aren't there? There's a problem, isn't there?
Nobody / everybody / someonethey: Nobody called, did they?
Negative words: never, nothing, no, hardlypositive tag: You never listen, do you?

Intonation and answers

Falling voice ↘ = I am sure, I just want agreement (Nice day, isn't it? ↘); rising voice ↗ = I really want to know (You haven't seen my keys, have you? ↗). Answer according to the facts, not the tag: "You're not from here, are you?" "No, I'm not." (true: I'm not from here) / "Yes, I am." (true: I am from here)

Typical mistakes: You like it, isn't it? → You like it, don't you? · She can swim, can she? → She can swim, can't she? · He has a car, hasn't he? → He has a car, doesn't he? (has = main verb) but He has got a car, hasn't he? · Tom is here, isn't Tom? → …, isn't he?

sebenta.title: Gerund and infinitive
sebenta.html:
The gerund is the -ing form of the verb used as a noun (swimming, reading). The infinitive is to + verb (to swim, to read). Which one you use depends on the word before it.

When to use the gerund (-ing)

UseExamples
as the subject of a sentenceSwimming is good for you. · Learning languages takes time.
after prepositions (at, in, of, for, about, before, after, without)I'm good at drawing. · She's interested in cooking. · Thanks for coming. · He left without saying goodbye.
after certain verbs: enjoy, like, love, hate, prefer, mind, finish, stop, keep, avoid, suggest, practise, miss, give up, can't stand, don't mind, feel likeI enjoy playing football. · She finished doing her homework. · Do you mind waiting? · I can't stand getting up early. · He gave up smoking.
after go for activities and after it's not worth, look forward togo swimming / shopping · It's not worth buying. · I'm looking forward to seeing you.

When to use the infinitive (to + verb)

UseExamples
after certain verbs: want, would like, would love, need, decide, hope, plan, promise, offer, refuse, agree, learn, manage, expect, seem, choose, forget, afford, pretendI want to go home. · She decided to stay. · We hope to win. · He promised to help. · They can't afford to buy it.
after adjectivesIt's easy to learn. · I'm happy to see you. · It was nice to meet you.
to express purpose (why?)I went to the shop to buy bread. · She's saving money to travel.
after too and enoughIt's too cold to go out. · He isn't old enough to drive.
verb + object + infinitive: want, ask, tell, help, teach, allow, expectI want you to listen. · She told me to wait. · He helped me (to) carry it.

Infinitive without to (bare infinitive)

After modal verbs (can, must, should, will…), after let and make + object, and after would rather / had better: You must go. · My parents let me stay up late. · The film made me cry. · You'd better hurry.

Both are possible

VerbsExamples
like, love, hate, prefer, start, begin, continue – little or no change of meaningI like reading / I like to read in bed. · It started raining / started to rain.
stop – different meaningHe stopped smoking. (he doesn't smoke any more) / He stopped to smoke. (he stopped in order to smoke)
remember / forget – different meaningI remember meeting her. (memory of the past) / Remember to lock the door. (don't forget your duty)
Typical mistakes: I enjoy to read → I enjoy reading · I want going → I want to go · I'm good at play → I'm good at playing · I must to go → I must go · She made me to laugh → She made me laugh.

sebenta.title: Word formation: prefixes and suffixes
sebenta.html:
A prefix goes before the word and changes its meaning (happy → unhappy). A suffix goes after the word and usually changes its class (noun, verb, adjective, adverb): care (n.) → careful (adj.) → carefully (adv.).

in-notincorrect, independent, invisible, informal

Suffixes

SuffixMakesExamples

-nessnouns from adjectiveshappiness, kindness, sadness, illness, darkness
-ship / -hoodnouns: state, relationfriendship, relationship; childhood, neighbourhood

-lessadjectives: withoutcareless, useless, homeless, hopeless, wireless

-yadjectives from nounssunny, rainy, healthy, noisy, lucky, friendly
-ing / -edadjectives from verbsboring film / bored student; exciting / excited; tiring / tired

–dangerdangerousdangerously
-ed vs -ing adjectives: -ed = how a person feels; -ing = what causes the feeling. I'm bored because the lesson is boring. Spelling: happy → happiness, beauty → beautiful, argue → argument, true → truly.
